newsitem.title: USA: Clean-up begins on flooded Arizona reservation.
newsitem.headline: Clean-up begins on flooded Arizona reservation.

text.p: Workers began cleaning up a flood-ravaged Indian reservation in northwestern Arizona late Tuesday as a helicopter airlifted 140 residents to safe ground, authorities said.
The 140, who found shelter in relatives' homes or a local gymnasium, were the last of hundreds of people to be evacuated.
Crews began efforts to repair sewer and water lines knocked out of service after floods caused by heavy rains hit a remote canyon village on the Havasupai Indian Reservation on Sunday.
Counting Tuesday's evacuees, more than 650 people had to be rescued. About 300 were tourists attending the annual Peach Festival who were forced out of the community's campgrounds.

The picturesque village, which is visited by thousands of tourists each year, is southwest of the Grand Canyon and accessible only by hiking, riding a mule or flying in a helicopter. The nearest road is eight miles away.

Bob McNichols, a superintendent with the Bureau of Indian Affairs, said he did not expect the affected sewer and water lines to be restored before next Monday. Water was being flown in for the roughly 235 residents who remained.
"There's been a lot of damage," McNichols told Reuters. "We've got our hands full doing what we have to do to try to get everything back into working condition."
Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt said Tuesday the federal government would provide $300,000 in short-term aid to the community from a special fund for severe natural disasters.
"Today's emergency assistance will meet the immediate needs of displaced tribal members until a more complete assessment can be made," Babbitt said.
More than 100 residents are being housed at an emergency shelter set up by the Red Cross at a gymnasium about 70 miles away in Peach Springs, Ariz.
On Sunday morning a storm dumped up to four inches of rain in two hours on the area. It was the third time in seven years that the remote village experienced severe flooding.
